clinicalPearls: An X-linked recessive disorder in which pigment deficiency is largely confined to the eye, with near-normal skin and hair pigmentation
Affected boys present with reduced acuity, congenital nystagmus, iris transillumination and photophobia
Foveal hypoplasia and hypopigmentation of the fundus with prominent choroidal vessels are characteristic
Misrouting of optic nerve fibres at the chiasm produces abnormal decussation, detectable on visual evoked potentials and associated with reduced stereopsis and strabismus
Caused by mutations in GPR143, encoding a G-protein-coupled receptor involved in melanosome biogenesis, giving giant melanosomes (macromelanosomes)
Carrier females may show a partial mud-splattered or mosaic fundus pigmentation and patchy iris transillumination due to lyonisation
Management is supportive with refractive correction, tinted lenses for photophobia, low-vision aids and strabismus care
reference.pathophysiology: Ocular albinism type 1 arises from mutations in the X-linked GPR143 gene, whose product regulates melanosome maturation and size within the retinal pigment epithelium and other melanocytes. Loss of function leads to abnormal, enlarged melanosomes and deficient ocular melanin, chiefly affecting the eye while skin and hair are relatively spared. Reduced retinal pigment impairs normal foveal development (foveal hypoplasia) and disturbs the guidance cues that determine crossing of ganglion cell axons at the chiasm, causing excessive decussation and misrouting. The combined effects produce nystagmus, subnormal acuity, iris transillumination and defective binocular vision. Female carriers show mosaic features owing to random X-inactivation.
additionalInvestigations: Dilated fundus examination for hypopigmentation and foveal hypoplasia
OCT of the macula to grade foveal hypoplasia
Visual evoked potentials to demonstrate chiasmal misrouting
Genetic testing of GPR143 and albinism gene panels
redFlags: Systemic bleeding tendency or recurrent infections suggesting syndromic albinism (Hermansky-Pudlak or Chediak-Higashi) rather than isolated ocular disease
Progressive rather than stable visual loss prompting reassessment for a retinal dystrophy
Marked asymmetry of findings requiring exclusion of other pathology
Failure to thrive or dysmorphism suggesting a broader syndrome
reference.prognosis: Vision is subnormal but usually stable, with acuity commonly in the low-vision range; most individuals function well with refractive correction, tints and low-vision support.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnosis in a boy with nystagmus because skin and hair look normal
Missing carrier status in the mother by not examining her iris and fundus
Failing to check for syndromic albinism when there is bruising or infection
Attributing poor acuity solely to nystagmus and neglecting foveal hypoplasia
references: Taylor & Hoyt's Paediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
management: No disease-specific treatment; optimise vision with full refractive correction and tinted or photochromic lenses to reduce photophobia
Low-vision aids and rehabilitation to support education and daily function
Orthoptic assessment and management of strabismus and nystagmus, with squint surgery or nystagmus null-point and head-posture surgery in selected cases
Regular ophthalmological follow-up to monitor acuity and refractive changes
Genetic counselling for X-linked GPR143 inheritance, with carrier testing of female relatives
